approved: Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would create a legal requirement for how commissioners are chosen for Australia's human rights watchdog.
The minister could only appoint someone if a public, competitive process had picked them.
No commissioner could serve longer than seven years in total, and the president would need specific expertise.
Codifies a requirement for merit-based and open selection processes for Australian Human Rights Commission members.
Limits the total term for a commissioner to seven years.
Requires the President to hold suitable qualifications, knowledge or experience.
Members and the President of the Australian Human Rights Commission, and the Minister responsible for appointments.
Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022 - Second Reading - Human Rights Commissioner for LGBTIQA+ people
Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022 - in Committee - Human Rights Commissioner for LGBTIQA+ people

The bill requires that all appointments to the Australian Human Rights Commission be made through a merit-based, publicly advertised selection process, limits terms to a maximum of seven years, and establishes consistent qualification requirements for the president and commissioners—addressing concerns that led to the deferral of the commission's A‑status reaccreditation in March 2022.

The coalition does not oppose the bill requiring merit-based, transparent appointments and a seven-year term limit for the Australian Human Rights Commission, arguing it is needed to retain A-status accreditation despite inconsistencies in the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions’ processes; the speaker defended the coalition’s human rights record, citing $120 million in Afghan aid, 30,000 humanitarian places, and Magnitsky-style sanctions, and thanked former commissioners including Ros Croucher, Kate Jenkins, and June Oscar.

The Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection And Appointment) Bill 2022 is necessary to ensure transparent, merit-based appointments and restore public trust, as the commission itself has long advocated—citing President Rosalind Croucher’s 1 August letter and the December 2021 Free and Equal position paper. The speaker also called for a national bill or charter of human rights to provide a legislative framework for rights and responsibilities.

The opposition supported the Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022, which introduces statutory merit-based appointment processes, and thanked Sex Discrimination Commissioner Kate Jenkins for her workplace culture report, noting the need for cultural change in Parliament.

The speech argued that the Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022 is needed to establish a merit-based selection process for commissioners and senior executives, addressing past politicisation that led to a deferral of A-status accreditation. It cited Grattan Institute data showing 21% of federal government board positions are political appointees, supported a new public appointments commissioner, and commended Sex Discrimination Commissioner Kate Jenkins as well as an amendment for a dedicated LGBTQI commissioner.

The Greens moved an amendment to the Australian Human Rights Commission Legislation Amendment (Selection and Appointment) Bill 2022 to establish a standalone LGBTQIA+ human rights commissioner, citing higher rates of homelessness and suicide among queer and trans people as evidence of urgent need.
